Could be a stupid post; could be super late to the game; but thought i'd share.

highly technical non-swe here. i've been vibing before karpathy coined the term, before mcp servers were publicly available, when openrouter's limits were nearly limitless, and when you could make 50 google accounts without kyc to tumble keys all day.

i've always struggled with maintaining my repos, or projects' codebases. probably because i never went to school, took a class, or even bothered to do any sort of extensive research beyond common practices, best standards... things of that nature.

since jev, though not being utilized for the scaffolding, I have been able to create a fully "deterministic" harness in terms of; when i want things done, how i want things done, common patterns, how to manage git state, and most importantly, just keep things neat and tidy.

"congrats you discovered hooks", well i have known about them, but due to my lack of swe-based jargon, there were things, back in the day; i didn't know how to put in words. sure i would use natural language but, that seemed to never work, or it did, but left edge cases. hooks only got me so far, or maybe my prompts only got me so far.

im primarily here to say:

1. the models capabilities of understanding it's own harness has DRASTICALLY improved. so much that I don't have to consistently feed its own documentation and steer into the right direction (what i think is the right direction?)

2. though I have been aware of classifiers, jev really fueled the fire for me to start classifying behaviors and operations within projects, the model provider harnesses i use day to day, work related pipelines..the whole 9 yards.

i've gone through countless skills, arrays of skills, huge skill repos, all to manage my workflows, project codebases, along with git state, and so on. sure it worked for awhile, but like, who wants to remember 17 different commands. we all know that stitching together 17 prompts into one skill, is bounded to a failure at some point or multiple points, so that's off the table.

now i'm sure it's a combination of poor prompting, lack of swe-based knowledge and understanding, models capability, and so on. 

but i'm here to tell you, if you haven't, or have but need to optimize, take a couple days and sit down and create a wireframe (like tldraw or something, all by hand, i know wtf?) and map out how you want your harness, pipeline, or project to behave. 

transform that little wireframe into a written spec, not a e2e-poc.md file, just plain text, good ol .md. 

why? so the agent isn't referencing an image every time you reference it, or the agent forgets all of sudden.

then plop that in a new cowork/work project and just sit down and talk, AGGRESSIVELY tell it to ask you questions, you're just exploring here, conversing, planning, speccing everything out. no coding, no files, no tests, nothing....i have been amazed at what I have achieved in terms of "configuring" how codex/claude code function and perform now, alongside a project that i have been wanting to build for over a year now.

though it has been possible, without AI, and with AI.. now it's even easier, & not to mention the "comfort" you get with jev classifying parts or most of what you want optimized/perfected, correctly? i think there's a beauty and a ugly side to being able to build and create said project, or product, and in the middle of the run, to create a script that makes sure it does X, Y, and Z. who tf is gonna sit there and baby sit a sanity check script? and if you dont, but want the comfort anyways - are you really going to send off another agent to sanity check the sanity checker?? (is that a loop? lmao) anyways, jev is cool for that, and some other things. this shit is just so cool.

go use jev alongside fable or astra, and just really hammer out what you want and need in terms of "determinism". stop building whatever you're building and make your system perform how you want it to perform.

looping on goals and bypass permissions gets shit done sure, but guess what, you come back and have to clean up a third of what it created alongside creating 3 more things just to enforce it's behavior to prevent that from happening again. silly.

a couple months ago, i would've said, yeah you need pi, or opencode to achieve full determinism, but i think that both major model providers have really come through in terms of intelligence, specifically in it's own ability to understand it's own harness (and as a matter of fact, the opposing teams' harness as well) + on top of their efforts of really curating their harnesses to be more and more customizable, via hooks, built-in classifiers, just the overall experience.

not really expecting much response from this. this just needed to get out <3

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

[📃 PAPER ALERT] Efficient, Property-Aligned Fan-Out Retrieval via RL-Compiled Diffusion - by Google Research & UIUC
arXiv: https://t.co/tt5pGCsbU3

When we search something broad like “camping gear,” we don't really want 10 slightly different tents.

We want:
tent + sleeping bag + stove + headlamp + other complementary things.
So modern search systems use query fan-out: take one broad query --> generate multiple sub-queries --> retrieve different aspects of the user's intent.

Sounds simple.

But there is a problem.

LLMs are autoregressive. To generate a good set of complementary, diverse AND database-grounded queries, they may need expensive inference-time reasoning.

And for a search system... do we really want the model to “think” heavily every single time someone searches?

I think NO.

This paper proposes : Retrieve-for-Train.

The idea is actually quite interesting:

Use expensive RL during TRAINING, not during INFERENCE.

The pipeline has 3 stages:

Train a Fan-Out Language Model (FOLM) using RL to generate useful sub-queries.

The reward jointly optimizes:

a. Groundedness: are the queries actually connected to items in the database?
b. Alignment: do they still follow the user's original intent?
c. Diversity: do they explore genuinely different semantic directions?

Use this RL-trained model to generate synthetic supervision.
So the expensive exploration happens offline.
No human-labelled property-aligned dataset is required.

Train a lightweight diffusion retriever on these generated targets.

At inference time, instead of autoregressively generating query after query...

the diffusion model generates multiple retrieval directions in parallel in embedding space.

Basically:

RL discovers the search strategy --> synthetic data stores it --> diffusion executes it cheaply.

Findings:
1. Zero-shot query fan-out helps, but it is not enough.
Normal LLMs often generate near-identical queries.
R4T instead learns complementary directions that cover more of the semantic space.
2. R4T improves retrieval quality over zero-shot fan-out and Best-of-N baselines.
The method was evaluated on fashion and music retrieval tasks where the desired output is a set rather than one correct item.
3. The diffusion retriever makes fan-out dramatically cheaper.

Their 53.9M-parameter diffusion model generates the retrieval directions non-autoregressively.

Reported fan-out latency:

LLM: ~1.46 s → ~50 s as batch size grows
Diffusion: ~0.07 s → 4.21 s

That is roughly 12×–20× faster.

[Interestingly]
The diversity reward is doing something more important than simply making the results diverse.

Without it, the RL model can reward-hack.

Optimizing only groundedness can produce nonsense strings that happen to land close to database embeddings.
Adding alignment alone can instead make the model collapse into repetitive paraphrases.

Groundedness + Alignment + Diversity work like counter-anchors that prevent these shortcuts.

I found this part particularly interesting because it shows how important reward interaction is in RL-based retrieval.

[In short] Instead of asking a large model to solve the same difficult search problem again and again at inference time...solve it during training and compile the learned behavior into a smaller model.

So the idea is almost:
System-2-like exploration during training → System-1-like retrieval during deployment.
And I think the broader idea may be even more interesting than retrieval itself.
Can we use RL to discover expensive behaviors once, turn those behaviors into training data, and then deploy a much cheaper model that reproduces them?

The paper from ICLR26 targets a basic weakness of preference learning: a binary judgment such as “trajectory A is better than B” says nothing about why it is better, allowing a reward model to exploit incidental correlations—for example, learning that moving left is desirable when the actual preference is avoiding collisions. 

ReCouPLe uses the accompanying natural-language rationale as a geometric constraint: the rationale is embedded as a direction {\psi} and each trajectory representation {\phi(\tau)} is decomposed into a component parallel to that direction and an orthogonal residual, encouraging the preference to be explained by features aligned with the stated reason rather than unrelated context. 

The reported experiments show up to a 1.5× improvement in reward accuracy under distribution shift and roughly 2× downstream policy performance on novel tasks, while semantically shared reasons such as “avoids collisions” can be reused across tasks without additional language-model fine-tuning; the released implementation includes ManiSkill3, MetaWorld, and offline-RL components. 

The broader idea is more interesting than the specific algorithm: language may serve as structure in representation space, not merely as another supervision label. That creates a direct bridge to causal representation learning, concept bottlenecks, disentanglement and reward hacking, and suggests a possible extension to LLM alignment in which reward models learn separate, reusable directions for honesty, harmlessness, factuality or other stated reasons instead of compressing everything into one opaque scalar score. 

But the word “causal” needs care here: projecting onto a rationale embedding does not establish that the direction corresponds to a genuine causal variable in the interventionist sense, and incorrect or post-hoc human rationales could simply produce more robustly encoded mistakes. 

The most important next step is therefore an explicit intervention/counterfactual test—change only the factor named by a rationale while holding the rest of the trajectory fixed and test whether the associated reward direction changes as predicted. If that works, preference learning could move from fitting black-box scores toward learning interpretable, manipulable and compositional reward factors.

Uni-LaDiR paper from UCSD and Meta has been sitting on my reading list, and after finally going through it, i feel it tackles something that’s annoyed researchers in multimodal research for ages.

Im talking about our obsession with shoving text tokens, image patches, and robot states into one giant sequence and pretending it's an elegant solution.

Every time we work with these interleaved models, it feels like they spend half their parameters just trying to babysit the handoffs between completely different modalities. 

You're forcing the network to solve format translation and actual problem logic at the exact same time.

The intuition the researchers bring here is that perception has to care about modalities, but the thinking itself shouldn't.

Instead of standard autoregression over mixed tokens, they project reasoning steps from across modalities into a unified, shared latent space. 

Then, they use a latent diffusion reasoner to generate entire chunks of thought tokens at once from the context. 

I really like this angle. 

Diffusion is just so much better suited for non deterministic branching than forcing a rigid, one-token-at-a-time syntax down the model's throat. 

In test time, it just synthesizes those latent thoughts on its own without needing teacher cues.

The empirical gains are hard to argue with. 

Its shows a 7.3% relative lift on math and logic across 11 VLM suites, plus a 6.1% bump on RLBench manipulation tasks for VLAs over strong baselines.

This paper genuinely tries to rethink multimodal reasoning mechanics from first principles instead of just dialing up scale on token soups. 

Well worth a look if you're working on VLMs or robotics.
